artists.biography: Todd Harry Rundgren (born June 22, 1948) is an American multi-instrumentalist, songwriter and record producer. Hailed in the early stage of his career as a new pop star, supported by the certified gold solo double LP Something/Anything? in 1972, his career has produced a diverse range of recordings as solo artist, and during the seventies and eighties with the band Utopia. He has also been prolific as a producer and engineer on the recorded work of other musicians.

A close listen to the album reveals the eccentricities and restless spirit that surges to the forefront on its follow-up, A Wizard, A True Star. Anyone expecting the third record of Something/Anything?, filled with variations on "I Saw the Light" and "Hello It\'s Me," will be shocked by A Wizard. As much a mind-f*ck as an album, A Wizard, A True Star rarely breaks down to full-fledged songs, especially on the first side, where songs and melodies float in and out of a hazy post-psychedelic mist. Stylistically, there may not be much new -- he touched on so many different bases on Something/Anything? that it\'s hard to expand to new territory -- but it\'s all synthesized and assembled in fresh, strange ways. Often, it\'s a jarring, disturbing listen, especially since Rundgren\'s humor has turned bizarre and insular. It truly takes a concerted effort on the part of the listener to unravel the record, since Rundgren makes no concessions -- not only does the soul medley jerk in unpredictable ways, but the anthemic closer, "Just One Victory," is layered with so many overdubs that it\'s hard to hear its moving melody unless you pay attention. And that\'s the key to understanding A Wizard, A True Star -- it\'s one of those rare rock albums that demands full attention and, depending on your own vantage, it may even reward such close listening.\n Read more on Last.fm. perplexity.description:
A Wizard, a True Star is Todd Rundgren's fourth studio album, released in March 1973 on Bearsville Records. Following the commercial success of his previous album Something/Anything, which yielded the top 5 hit "Hello It's Me," Rundgren deliberately pursued an experimental direction with this record. Created at his newly built Secret Sound studio in New York, the album represents a deliberate rejection of commercial conventions, arriving with an explicit "no singles" policy despite its 55-minute runtime. The first side features a densely layered sonic palette combining rock guitars, synthesizers, and AM pop elements in what Rundgren described as an attempt to "imprint the chaos in [his] head onto a record without trying to clean it up."

Musically, A Wizard, a True Star occupies a distinctive space within psychedelic and progressive rock, characterized by its ambitious studio experimentation and genre-blending approach. The album's structure and ambition reflect Rundgren's willingness to explore diverse sonic possibilities, balancing experimental complexity with moments of humor and accessibility. This "kitchen sink" approach—where the artist exercises complete creative freedom in the studio—established a template that would influence subsequent generations of artists, including Trent Reznor and other experimental musicians.

The album received mixed critical reception upon release, peaking at number 86 on the Billboard 200 chart in May 1973. Despite its commercial underperformance relative to Something/Anything, the record has since been recognized as a significant achievement in psychedelic rock history. Rundgren himself has expressed pride in the album as "an act of tyranny after having achieved commercial success," noting that while it initially cost him approximately half his audience, it became influential among artists seeking to push creative boundaries.
